t:
Section 46301 is amended—

    (1) in subsection (a)(1)(A) by striking “46302, 46303, or”; 
    (2) in subsection (d)(7)(A) by striking “an individual” the first place it appears and inserting “a person”; and 
    (3) in subsection (g) by inserting “or the Administrator” after “Secretary”.

fable.w: This section makes only technical wording amendments to section 46301: it strikes cross-references, replaces "an individual" with "a person", and adds "or the Administrator" after "Secretary". The tempting reading is that changing the penalty provisions implies hearings or a right to challenge, but the text itself sets up no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to sue. No party outside the federal government is brought into any federal decision.

qwen_block.w: This section consists entirely of technical amendments to existing statutory text, changing specific words or phrases. It does not establish any new process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, advisory boards, or hearings. The changes are purely editorial or definitional within the statute itself.

opus.w: This section only makes technical edits to Section 46301: it strikes cross-references, changes 'an individual' to 'a person', and adds 'or the Administrator' after 'Secretary'. The text itself creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or new right to sue. One could argue that subsection (g) deals with judicial review and that this edit widens it. But the edit only changes which official is covered and does not, on its face, grant an outside party a right to challenge a decision.
opus.s: in subsection (g) by inserting “or the Administrator” after “Secretary”
opus.b:
1. **The tempting reading:** Section 46301 of title 49 governs civil penalties. From background knowledge, subsection (g) deals with judicial review of orders, and subsection (d) involves notice and hearings. So adding "or the Administrator" to subsection (g) could look like it gives outside parties a new right to sue over the Administrator's orders.

2. **Why that fails:** Nothing in the text itself sets up a hearing, comment period, consultation, advisory body, or right to sue. These are technical edits that strike or insert words. Even if subsection (g) is about review, these edits only change which official the existing provision covers. Under the definition, that is closer to describing litigation than granting an outside party a right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section consists solely of textual amendments to another statute, specifically striking and inserting words. It does not establish any process for consultation or coordination with parties outside the federal government, such as states, tribes, the public, or private entities. The insertion of 'the Administrator' likely refers to a federal official, keeping the interaction within the government. Therefore, it does not involve participation as defined.
